title: Apartment valuation: what determines market value
description: How an apartment is valued: location, building condition, floor area and comparable evidence. Find out what to prepare before commissioning a valuation.
intro: Apartment valuation involves more than multiplying the floor area by a price per square metre. Even apartments of the same size in the same neighbourhood can have different market values. The differences arise from the specific location, building, condition, legal information and the market evidence relevant to the valuation date.

sections.title: Location means more than the name of a neighbourhood
paragraphs: An apartment's address is a starting point, but the analysis does not end with an average price for a street or neighbourhood. Access, the surrounding environment, the building's position in relation to the street and everyday usability all matter. Proximity to the sea or a particular view may be important to a buyer, but its effect should be considered against relevant market evidence.

A higher floor does not automatically mean a higher value. The lift, the building's overall condition, the layout and other characteristics also need to be considered. Useful comparisons involve properties that resemble your apartment in their main features; listings connected only by the name of the city are not enough.

sections.title: Floor area, renovation and the building are considered together
paragraphs: For a valuation, it is important to relate the area recorded in the documents, the plan provided and the description of the apartment as it actually stands. Tell the valuer at the outset about any alterations, extensions or other changes, and share the available documentation.

Money spent on renovation does not always increase market value by the same amount. The valuation considers the condition and quality of the work, the practicality of the layout and market demand. It should also be agreed in advance whether the assignment includes furniture, appliances, a parking space or another separate asset.

sections.title: Why an average of a few listing prices is not enough
paragraphs: A listing shows a seller's offer. It does not, by itself, confirm that a transaction took place at that price. When assessing comparable information, its date, reliability, the property's condition and any differences in transaction terms all matter.

If the apartment is rented out, lease information may also be needed. Expected short-term rental income and money actually received are not the same. The information required depends on the purpose of the valuation and the agreed scope of work.

sections.title: How to start an apartment valuation
paragraphs: At the first discussion, explain why you need the report: a sale, a purchase, a financing matter or another purpose. Specify the valuation date required and who will receive the report. If the recipient has particular requirements, confirm its acceptance conditions before placing an order.

You can send GB Valuation a brief description of the property. We consider valuation enquiries from across Georgia. After reviewing the documents, inspection needs and assignment, we agree the scope of work, fee and delivery time.
bullets: The address or cadastral code and an available extract from the Public Registry;
A plan, floor-area information and recent photographs;
The purpose of the valuation, the required date and the report recipient's requirements.

takeaway: A supported apartment valuation draws on analysis of the specific property and relevant market evidence. To begin, prepare the address, a description of the property and the intended use of the report.

title: Documents for a property valuation: how to prepare
description: Registry extract, cadastral code, plan, photographs and purpose: a practical guide to preparing for an apartment, land or commercial property valuation.
intro: A property valuation is easier to start when information about the property has been gathered in advance. Initial documents help the valuer establish what is being valued, for what purpose and what work will be needed. There is no identical mandatory package for every case: the requirements depend on the property and the assignment.

sections.title: Start by identifying the property accurately
paragraphs: Along with the address, it is useful to provide the cadastral code. This helps connect the property with its registration information. Prepare any available extract from the Public Registry and tell the valuer about any restrictions, ownership share or other significant circumstances you are aware of.

If several apartments, plots or commercial units share one address, specify which one the assignment concerns. Land, a building, a parking space and equipment are not automatically treated as a single valuation subject. The property included in the valuation should be clearly described from the outset.

sections.title: Plans and photographs help describe the actual condition
paragraphs: For an apartment or building, prepare a plan and floor-area information if these materials are available. Photographs should preferably be recent and show the property's actual condition. Mention alterations, unfinished work or significant damage in advance.

Photographs and documents do not automatically remove the need for an inspection. The valuer determines what additional information or access is needed for the assignment. Agree in advance who will arrange entry and whether all areas relevant to the valuation will be accessible.

sections.title: What else may be needed for each property type
paragraphs: For a land plot, a cadastral plan, any available survey information, a description of access and available planning documents are particularly useful. If you are considering a specific development, share the existing documentary basis with the valuer and distinguish planned circumstances from those already confirmed.

For rented commercial premises, lease agreements, information on rent received and a summary of expenses may be needed. For plant and equipment, an asset list, model details, technical descriptions and condition information can be useful. The final list is agreed for the specific assignment.
bullets: Apartment or house: a plan, floor-area information and a description of the condition and alterations;
Land: a cadastral plan, boundary information and existing documents relating to use;
Commercial premises: relevant leases, rent information and operating expenses.

sections.title: Provide the purpose and valuation date along with the documents
paragraphs: The day a report is prepared and the date at which the property's value is assessed may differ. If you need a valuation for an earlier period, say so at the outset and prepare any available information about the property's condition at that time. Today's photographs cannot always describe its past condition.

If the report will be submitted to a bank, a court or another institution, obtain its requirements before commissioning the work. The choice of valuer, scope and format should be consistent with those requirements. You can send GB Valuation your initial information at the first enquiry; we will clarify any further materials when discussing the assignment.

takeaway: Start with the cadastral code or address, available registration information, a plan and photographs. Include the valuation's purpose, the required valuation date and the report recipient's requirements.

title: Asking price and market value: why they differ
description: Why a listing price does not establish a property's market value. Learn how comparable properties, dates and transaction terms are considered.
intro: The amount shown in a property listing is the seller's offer. Market value is assessed as at a specific date within an agreed valuation assignment. The two amounts may be close, but treating them as automatically equivalent provides an insufficient basis for a decision.

sections.title: What a listing tells us, and what remains unknown
paragraphs: A listing shows the price an owner is asking at a particular moment. That amount may allow for negotiation, or the offer may include particular conditions. A listing alone often does not tell us the price or terms on which a transaction was completed.

The same property may appear in several listings with different descriptions or prices. Counting these records as separate properties distorts the picture. The listing's relevance in time also matters: an old offer may no longer reflect the market at the valuation date.

sections.title: Both the properties and their terms need to be comparable
paragraphs: When comparing two apartments, the city and floor area are only the beginning. Attention is paid to location, building and apartment condition, floor, layout, legal characteristics and the date of the information. For commercial premises, the lease, usability and expenses may also be important.

It matters what the price includes. A furnished and an unfurnished apartment, with or without a separate parking space, are not offered on the same terms. The valuer selects relevant evidence and considers the differences; taking an average of a few random prices cannot replace that work.
bullets: Is the information current and verifiable?
How similar is the comparable to the property being valued?
Does the price relate to an offer or a confirmed transaction?
Which property, rights and additional terms are included in the amount?

sections.title: Why value is not the same as the amount you have spent
paragraphs: Purchase and renovation costs are important information for the owner, but the market is not determined solely by the total costs. A buyer's choice is affected by the property's practical use, condition, location and available alternatives. Improvements tailored to a particular taste will not create the same additional value for every buyer.

Neither a quickly accepted offer nor a long-running listing, on its own, is enough to draw a conclusion. The outcome is affected by sale terms, the quality of information and agreement with the buyer. A valuation helps support a decision, but it does not guarantee a future sale price.

sections.title: How to use a valuation when making a decision
paragraphs: When reading a valuation report, look beyond the final figure to the date, purpose, description of the property, information used and significant assumptions. If the property's condition or the market has changed, the suitability of using an older report should be reconsidered.

When contacting GB Valuation, tell us whether you are buying, selling or need a report for another purpose. Provide a description of the property and the terms of any existing offer. This allows us to discuss the specific assignment and agree the scope of work.

takeaway: A listing price is an offer; a supported valuation requires analysis of relevant evidence, differences and the agreed date. Always read the report's conditions as well as its final figure.

title: Land valuation: what to consider
description: Access, designated use, terrain, utilities and documented use all matter in land valuation. See what information to prepare for an enquiry.
intro: A land plot's value is not determined solely by its area and the name of the village or city. Even adjacent plots may differ in access, terrain, legal position and potential use. In a land valuation, these differences are considered using specific documents and relevant market evidence.

sections.title: Cadastral information is the starting point
paragraphs: Prepare the plot's cadastral code, any available registry extract and the cadastral plan. It is important to establish which land and rights are included in the assignment, what area is registered and what circumstances the valuer should consider. If only a share or a group of plots is being valued, describe this in advance.

A boundary indicated on site by the owner and the documentary information may require further clarification. Any available survey materials and boundary information are useful. A valuation report does not replace the process of establishing boundaries or resolving ownership questions.

sections.title: Access, shape and terrain affect usability
paragraphs: Equal areas do not mean equal practical opportunities. A plot's shape, slope, connection to the road and access conditions affect its use and attractiveness. Relying only on the price per square metre is therefore insufficient when choosing comparable land plots.

For utilities, an accurate description is useful: which networks are directly beside the plot, what information is available about connection and what is documented. A network in the surrounding area and a confirmed connection opportunity for the plot are not the same. Significant uncertainty should be reflected in the valuation through an appropriate assumption or limitation.

sections.title: Distinguish a planned project from documented use
paragraphs: When buying land, people often consider a house, hotel or another future development. An idea does not automatically confirm that such construction is possible. The registered designation, existing restrictions and available planning information are important for a valuation.

If documents support a particular use, provide them to the valuer. If the information has yet to be obtained, make that clear at the outset. A valuation does not replace permission from the competent authority or treat an unconfirmed future possibility as an established fact.

sections.title: What to send when discussing a land valuation
paragraphs: The purpose and valuation date are essential initial information for land as well. Considering a current transaction and determining value at a past date, for example, may require different evidence. Also explain whether buildings or other assets on the land are included in the assignment.

GB Valuation considers land valuation enquiries from across Georgia. Send us the location and available information so that we can clarify any additional materials, the need for an inspection and the terms of the assignment.
bullets: Cadastral code, registry extract and plan;
A description of the location and access, with recent photographs;
Existing survey and planning documents;
The valuation's purpose, date and a description of the property included.

takeaway: Along with area, the specific plot's physical and legal characteristics are central to land valuation. The potential for future use should be considered against appropriate documentation.

title: Commercial property valuation: rent, location and expenses
description: Valuing an office, shop or service premises: why leases, vacancy, expenses and relevant market evidence matter.
intro: When valuing commercial premises, their use and attractiveness to tenants matter alongside their floor area. Offices, shops and service spaces meet different needs. A supported view of value combines location, property condition, relevant market information and, where needed, lease data.

sections.title: The importance of location depends on the premises' function
paragraphs: For retail premises, visibility from the street, the entrance and customer access may be important. For an office, the focus may be on access, layout and building services. Not every nearby commercial property is therefore equally useful as a comparable.

A valuation considers the actual condition and use supported by documentation. If the space needs alterations, the existing condition and relevant information should be described. The owner's future plans and the possibilities already available need to be distinguished.

sections.title: Contract rent does not always show the whole picture
paragraphs: For rented premises, the valuer may need the lease agreement, payment terms, duration and information on rent received. The amount in the contract is considered alongside relevant market rent and other conditions. Agreed rent may also differ from the income actually received.

When considering an income approach, potential vacancy and relevant operating expenses matter. Simply multiplying annual rent by an arbitrarily selected number does not produce a supported valuation. The evidence and assumptions used should fit the specific property and assignment.
bullets: The lease's remaining term and significant conditions;
Information on rent charged and received, where available;
A distinction between expenses borne by the owner and by the tenant;
Occupancy and any vacant areas.

sections.title: Vacant and leased premises have different conditions
paragraphs: The existing tenant, remaining lease term and contract conditions may be important to the valuation. For vacant premises, attention is paid to condition, possible use and relevant market evidence. The assignment should clearly state the circumstances on which the valuation is based.

The value of commercial premises is not automatically the value of the business operating there. Land and buildings, furniture, equipment, inventory and business-related rights are different assets. What is included should be defined in advance so that nothing is omitted or counted twice.

sections.title: How to prepare to commission a valuation
paragraphs: Send us the cadastral code or address, an available registry extract and a plan. Briefly describe the use, condition, occupancy and purpose of the valuation. If there is a tenant, prepare the relevant agreements and a summary of rent and expenses.

When discussing work with GB Valuation, the report's purpose, valuation date, scope, fee and delivery time are agreed in advance. If the report is for a particular institution, clarify its acceptance requirements before commissioning the work and share them with us.

takeaway: Commercial property valuation combines property characteristics and relevant market evidence. Leases and expenses are considered in context, while the premises and the business operating within them should be defined separately.

sections.title: Timing also depends on information and arranging access

Knowing the measured area alone does not establish a property's value. Two apartments of equal size may differ in location, building, condition and other features. A measured plan can therefore be useful evidence for a valuation, but it does not replace a valuation report.

sections.title: Why compare the actual condition with the documents?
paragraphs: If an old plan no longer matches the current layout, or you have several different area figures, mention this at the outset. title: Business valuation: company value and ownership interests
description: Valuing a business, company or ownership interest: how it differs from asset valuation, what information is needed and how the scope is agreed.
intro: Business valuation involves more than adding up the prices of a company's property and equipment. The subject may be an operating business, the company's total equity or a particular ownership interest. GB Valuation also considers business valuation assignments; we first clarify what is being valued, for what purpose and as at which date.

sections.title: Distinguish the business's value from the value of its assets
paragraphs: Buildings, plant and other assets are part of a business, but an operating activity is not always equivalent to selling them separately. A company may have income, liabilities, contracts and operating circumstances that affect the overall picture. Valuing individual assets does not therefore automatically mean valuing the entire business.

Before work begins, it should be clear whether the whole business or a specific ownership interest is being considered. The rights attached to that interest also matter. Its value cannot always be established simply by multiplying company value by a percentage; the valuation considers the particular rights and agreed conditions.

sections.title: Why do you need a business or ownership-interest valuation?
paragraphs: A valuation may be needed when considering a sale, purchase, new partner, transfer of an ownership interest or another decision. The purpose determines what information needs to be collected and how the assignment is defined. If a particular party will receive the report, its requirements should also be clarified in advance.

The valuation date is important for a business. A company's financial position and operating prospects change over time. The information and assumptions used in the report relate to a particular date and agreed purpose; achieving the same price in a future transaction is not guaranteed.

sections.title: What information helps assess value?
paragraphs: The assignment may require financial statements, a breakdown of income and expenses, a description of liabilities, an asset list and significant contracts. Alongside historical results, supported forecasts may be considered. One-off income should be distinguished from results that the business can generate repeatedly.

Risks matter too: reliance on key customers or the owner, changes in costs and the sustainability of income. The information supplied for a valuation needs an appropriate basis. The final materials list and arrangements for sharing confidential information are agreed for the specific assignment.
bullets: A brief description of the company and ownership interest to be valued;
Available financial information and operating history;
Significant assets, liabilities and contracts;
The purpose, valuation date and report recipient.

sections.title: The approach fits the business and available evidence
paragraphs: Comparable market information, analysis of future cash flows or asset-based analysis may help assess value. The method chosen depends on the activity, assignment and evidence available. Applying a single multiple to every business does not provide sufficient support.

When contacting GB Valuation, send us the business sector and a brief description, and state whether the whole company or an ownership interest is being valued. We will clarify the scope of full business valuation separately from the valuation of individual assets. The information required, fee and delivery time are agreed after the assignment is discussed.
